summary:
Sudden cardiac death occurs when a person dies unexpectedly as a result of a heart condition or disorder. Life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias are often the cause, as they prevent the heart from pumping blood through the body at all, or from pumping enough blood. Without immediate treatment, these arrhythmias can lead to death within a matter of minutes.
People with severely impaired heart pump function are among those at increased risk. In some patients, heart function may improve again during the course of treatment. For this reason, in certain situations, a wait-and-see approach is adopted to determine whether a permanent implantable defibrillator is required. This device is implanted in the body and can detect and treat life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.
During this waiting period, or in the case of other medical indications, a portable defibrillator vest may be used. It continuously monitors the heart rhythm and can deliver an electric shock in the event of certain life-threatening arrhythmias. For reliable protection, it is essential that the vest is worn as continuously as possible.
However, some patients choose not to use a defibrillator vest or wear it only irregularly. The reasons for this have not yet been sufficiently investigated. The aim of this study is therefore to gain a better understanding of the factors that influence the decision for or against a defibrillator vest and the circumstances that facilitate or hinder its regular use in everyday life. Furthermore, the study aims to investigate how information and support for those affected can be improved.

Adult patients with a medical indication for a defibrillator vest are eligible to take part in the study. This applies regardless of whether they decide to wear the vest or not. Recruitment is taking place mainly at the German Heart Centre at Charité in Berlin. Participation by patients from other treatment centres is also possible. Participation is voluntary and requires written consent.

The study consists of two phases that build on one another. In the first phase, face-to-face interviews will be conducted with patients after they have decided whether or not to use a defibrillator vest. Relatives and treating doctors will also be interviewed. The focus will be on the reasons behind the decision, personal expectations and concerns, as well as experiences with the defibrillator vest in everyday life. For patients who wear a vest, further experiences and any difficulties encountered will be recorded after approximately three months.

Based on the interviews, questionnaires will be developed and subsequently administered to a larger group of patients. In this second phase, the responses from the questionnaires will be compared with medical information and, for those wearing a defibrillator vest, with the actual usage data recorded. The aim is to investigate which factors are associated with the decision to use the vest and its regular use.

The study does not involve any additional treatment or changes to medical care. The results are intended to help better understand the needs and concerns of those affected. On this basis, ways can be developed to improve patient education, shared decision-making and support whilst using a defibrillator vest.v

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Hospitalized patients with heart failure and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF <35%).
2. Medical indication for temporary use of a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) as a bridging strategy until a decision regarding ICD implantation is made.
3. Ability to provide written informed consent independently.
4. Sufficient cognitive abilities to appropriately handle and use the WCD.
5. Treatment at the Deutsches Herzzentrum der Charité (DHZC), Campus Mitte (and, if applicable during the course of the study, Campus Virchow-Klinikum and Campus Benjamin Franklin).
6. Willingness to participate in interviews and complete study-specific questionnaires.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Lack of capacity to provide informed consent, e.g., due to cognitive impairment.
2. Insufficient language proficiency to participate in the study without translation assistance.
3. Acute psychiatric disorders that interfere with study participation.
4. Terminal illness or an estimated life expectancy of less than three months.
5. Pre-existing ICD implantation or an immediate indication for ICD implantation without a planned bridging period.
